st.headline: Taiwan dollar bulls look past AI-led selloff to year-end rally
st.teaser: Analysts say record trade surpluses and AI-related exports continue to generate underlying Taiwan dollar support.
fullText: TAIPEI – The Taiwan dollar’s weakness led by global jitters over the artificial intelligence trade is masking the island’s underlying economic resilience that favours the currency’s rally into year-end, analysts say.

While the currency has come under intense pressure in recent sessions, Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation and ING Bank see it rebounding to 31.60 and 31.50, respectively, implying an appreciation about 3% from current levels.
Underscoring those projections are Taiwan’s robust economic growth and current account surplus.

Even though doubts over lofty AI stock valuations continue to drive outflows and weigh on the exchange rate in the short term, analysts expect fundamental trade support to prevail over the coming months.
“Record trade surpluses and AI-related exports continue to generate underlying Taiwan dollar support,” said Lin Li, head of global markets research for Asia at MUFG Bank.
“But foreign portfolio outflows, outward investment and the large US dollar-Taiwan dollar yield differential is creating offsetting US dollar demand at the moment.”
Li sees the Taiwan dollar appreciating to 31.8 per greenback by year-end before gaining further to 30.9 by the end of June 2027.
The island’s currency dropped to the weakest since April 2025 on Oct 19 after global funds sold local stocks every day earlier in October.

Taiwan’s current account surplus reached a record high of nearly US$70 billion (S$89.6 billion) in late 2025, buoyed by unprecedented global demand for advanced chips, before narrowing moderately in recent months.
At the same time, officials raised the island’s full-year economic growth forecast to more than 10%, putting the technology hub on track for its first double-digit expansion since 2010.

Still, those underlying strengths are clashing with a wave of foreign capital flight. Foreign investors sold NT$302.6 billion (S$11.9 billion) of Taiwan equities on Oct 15, the largest daily outflow on record, pushing the Taiwan dollar to within striking distance of its year-to-date low of around 32.50 per US dollar.

While analysts do not view that level as a rigid line in the sand for policymakers, they are watching it closely as a comfortable zone for the monetary authority known as the Central Bank of the Republic of China or CBC.

“The CBC will attempt to keep the Taiwan dollar relatively rangebound,” said Lynn Song, chief economist for Greater China at ING Bank. “I don’t think it is a firm line in the sand to defend, but it does seem that 31.5-32.5 range has been comfortable for them so far in 2026.”

For Jiuk Choi, Asia Pacific macro strategist at State Street Bank & Trust, the CBC is more likely to focus on easing currency volatility than target a certain level. “That said, we think the 32.4-32.5 range is an important level for US dollar-Taiwan dollar, as it marks the year-to-date high in 2026,” he said.
Beyond concerns over the tech sector, elevated crude prices are adding further pressure on the Taiwan dollar as the island is an energy importer.

Moreover, US 10-year Treasury yields sit roughly 300 basis points above similar-tenor Taiwanese sovereign bonds, offering a compelling yield pickup that continues to fuel broad US dollar strength at the expense of regional currencies.
“Near-term headwinds include foreign equity outflows and a strong US dollar amid a hawkish Federal Reserve,” said Trang Le, foreign exchange and rates specialist, LGT Private Banking.

“Even so, strong export momentum, robust external balances and the AI-driven semiconductor cycle leave the medium-term bias tilted toward Taiwan dollar appreciation. We expect volatility rather than sustained weakness to be the dominant theme,” she said.

Currency traders are watching earnings reports from major semiconductor manufacturers, which strategists view as the next key catalyst for cross-border equity flows and currency volatility. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing delivered a better-than-expected revenue outlook on Oct 15, yet it failed to fully calm market worries over the broader AI buildout.

“Upcoming global tech earnings could increase Taiwan dollar volatility, particularly given the market’s heightened sensitivity to AI-related capex, profitability, and Chinese competition,” said Choi from State Street Bank & Trust.
He sees near-term room for Taiwan dollar weakness on AI trade doubts, but expects a recovery to 31.80 per US dollar by year-end.

“We see Taiwan dollar is one of the best hedge currencies to US dollar strength as capital and current account flows remain strong while it has one of the lowest volatilities across emerging markets,” he said. BLOOMBERG

cna.headline: After years of frustration, Davidovich Fokina wins third title of 2026
cna.teaser: After years of frustration, Davidovich Fokina wins third title of 2026
fullText: Oct 19 : Alejandro Davidovich Fokina waited seven years for an ATP Tour title then three came along at once.

The Spaniard, who made his tour debut in April 2019, captured the Shanghai Masters title with a 1-6 7-6(5) 6-4 win over compatriot Rafael Jodar on Sunday, earning him a third career trophy after his wins in Chengdu last month and Mallorca in June.
"I cannot describe with words what I achieved in this Chinese swing," Davidovich Fokina, who lost his first five ATP finals, told a press conference.

"I never thought I would have two titles after two months out. But I'm really, really happy. I think my team (were) pushing me. It was difficult when I was at home, and they were pushing me very hard.
The 27-year-old, whose win in Chengdu came in his first tournament back after a two-month layoff due to a back injury, has risen from number 26 in the world rankings to a career-high 13.
A single handpicked story that we think you shouldn't miss. Just one a day.

listening.title: Singapore Steps Up Regional Clean Energy Imports
listening.transcript: Singapore is accelerating its transition toward clean energy by importing low-carbon electricity from neighbouring Southeast Asian nations. Conditional approvals have recently been granted for large-scale power projects in Indonesia and Vietnam. Analysts note that diversifying energy sources is essential for the land-scarce island nation to achieve its target of net-zero emissions by 2050.

economistArticle.title: The Italian Job: Mediterranean Firms Hunt in Germany
paras: When UniCredit unexpectedly built a sizeable stake in Commerzbank, Germany’s second-largest lender, politicians in Berlin reacted with predictable dismay. Chancellor Olaf Scholz described the move as an unfriendly act, warning against hostile takeovers in the financial sector. Yet UniCredit’s bold maneuver is far from an isolated corporate raid. Across energy, manufacturing, and logistics, Italian enterprises are quietly devouring German assets at an unprecedented tempo.

For decades, the economic relationship between the two nations was defined by a clear hierarchy. Formidable German conglomerates viewed Italy primarily as a supplier of specialized components or a sun-drenched holiday destination. Today, however, sluggish growth and exorbitant energy tariffs in Germany have weakened indigenous champions, leaving vulnerable targets exposed to aggressive foreign suitors with healthier balance sheets.

Consider the energy sector, where Italian giants like Enel have expanded their reach across Central Europe. Italian manufacturing groups, buoyed by nimble supply chains and lower operational costs, are acquiring distressed medium-sized industrial firms across Baden-Württemberg and Bavaria. Italian capital is no longer mere emergency relief; it is driving strategic consolidation in the heartland of European industry.

German commentators lament this trend as an erosion of national industrial sovereignty. However, pragmatic economists argue that cross-border consolidation is precisely what the European single market was created to foster. If European firms are to compete against American tech behemoths and state-subsidised Chinese rivals, scale matters far more than national pride.

As Berlin grapples with structural stagnation, Milan’s corporate titans are showing no signs of slowing down. The assault on Commerzbank may be generating the loudest headlines, but the broader Italian acquisition spree signals a historic rebalancing of power within Europe’s economic core.
economistArticle.cn:
当意信银行（UniCredit）出人意料地增持德国第二大银行商业银行（Commerzbank）的大量股份时，柏林的政治家们做出了可预测的惊慌反应。总理奥拉夫·朔尔茨将此举描述为非友善行为，警告要防范金融领域的敌意收购。然而，意信银行的大胆举动绝非孤立的企业突袭。在能源、制造和物流领域，意大利企业正在以前所未有的速度悄然吞噬德国资产。

几十年来，两国之间的经济关系一直由清晰的等级制度决定。令人敬畏的德国企业集团主要将意大利视为专业零部件的供应商或阳光明媚的度假胜地。然而，如今德国缓慢的增长和高昂的能源关税削弱了本土冠军企业，使脆弱的目标暴露在拥有更健康资产负债表的积极外国求购者面前。

以能源领域为例，意大网巨人如Enel已将其触角延伸至中欧各地。凭借灵活的供应链和较低的运营成本，意大利制造集团正在收购巴登-符腾堡州和巴伐利亚州陷入困境的中型工业企业。意大利资本不再仅仅是紧急救济；它正在推动欧洲工业核心地带的战略整合。

德国评论员痛惜这一趋势是国家工业主权的削弱。然而，务实的经济学家认为，跨国整合正是建立欧洲单一市场所要促进的。如果欧洲企业要与美国科技巨头和受国家补贴的中国对手竞争，规模比国家自豪感更为重要。

随着柏林努力应对结构性停滞，米兰的企业巨头们没有表现出任何放缓的迹象。对商业银行的进攻可能引发了最响亮的新闻头条，但更广泛的意大利收购潮预示着欧洲经济核心内部力量的历史性重新平衡。
